rationale: Sambale, Definition 7.1, gives formal Laurent series as sums with an integer lower exponent bound and the usual finite-convolution operations; Dales, section 2.4/2.5, presents the same object as the Hahn field on Z, with least-support valuation and its ordered-field structure. The item changes X to t^{-1}, represents series as functions Z -> R, and packages support, monomials, constants, valuation, leading coefficient, and the lexicographic positive cone into one definition. Those are convention and packaging changes, not a new construction.

Sambale, Definition 7.1 and Theorem 7.2, state the lower-bounded Laurent-series operations, note that every coefficient convolution is finite, and obtain a commutative ring; Dales states the same finite Hahn convolution and identifies the Z case with formal Laurent series. The local Statement additionally spells out support bounds, shifts, constants, and the least-support index, so it is a semantically faithful expansion rather than an exact transcription. The proof adapts Sambale's coefficientwise finite-convolution ring proof and expands its support and monomial bookkeeping.

The Encyclopedia of Mathematics defines the formal Laurent-series valuation by the least exponent, and Dales gives the Hahn valuation on the same Z-indexed field. Sambale's Lemmas 2.2 and 2.8 prove the product least-index law and the unequal-valuation sum law for formal series. The item expands those sourced arguments into leading-coefficient and cancellation cases.

Sambale, Theorem 7.2, states that K((X)) is the fraction field of K[[X]] and hence a field, and proves inversion by shifting a nonzero Laurent series to a power-series unit; the Encyclopedia of Mathematics gives the same field statement. The local theorem fixes R, writes X=t^{-1}, and expands the unit inverse as a coefficientwise finite geometric construction. Its proof adapts the sourced shift-and-invert argument and supplies an explicit geometric-series verification.

Dales defines Hahn series by well-ordered support, finite convolution, least-support valuation, and the leading-term order, and states that the resulting Hahn algebra is an ordered field; section 2.5 identifies the value group Z case with formal Laurent series. The item specializes to R((t^{-1})) and adds the absolute-value and constant-embedding clauses. The positive-cone verification is a local proof rather than an identifiable sourced proof.

Dales presents R((X)) as the Z-valued Hahn field with least-support valuation and leading-term order, the standard non-Archimedean Laurent-series construction. The item's inequalities t>n, the decreasing monomials, their countable coinitiality among positive elements, and the coefficient/valuation threshold equivalence are direct specialized formulations of that structure. The detailed inequality proof is locally constructed.

The Rutgers notes state and prove that every complete ordered field is Archimedean by taking a supremum of its canonical naturals; Dales supplies the non-Archimedean ordered Hahn/Laurent field. The corollary is their standard contrapositive specialized to K and gives the canonical naturals as the explicit bounded set. Its leading-coefficient halving argument adapts the sourced supremum-of-naturals proof to the Laurent order.

The University of Tennessee notes define Cauchy sequences and Cauchy completeness in an arbitrary ordered field using every positive field element as epsilon. The item faithfully compiles those definitions with the standard ordered-field notions of convergence, monotonicity, boundedness, subsequence, and interval, and adds a Laurent-field warning about rational-only thresholds. The compilation and notation differ, but the mathematical notions are standard and semantically unchanged.

The Encyclopedia of Mathematics states that the formal Laurent-series field k((X)) with its least-exponent valuation is a discretely valued complete field; Dales identifies the R, value-group-Z instance and its leading-term ordered-field structure. In this instance the monomials form a countable order-neighborhood base, so valuation completeness and the item's ordered-field Cauchy completeness are semantically the same. The proof adapts Sambale's coefficient-stabilization proof of completeness for formal power series and adds the Laurent-specific uniform lower-support argument plus the order-threshold conversion.

The Encyclopedia of Mathematics states the Cantor completeness criterion: decreasing nonempty closed sets with diameters tending to zero have nonempty intersection in a complete metric space. The item is the ordered-field interval specialization, with diameter b_n-a_n measured in K, and strengthens nonemptiness to uniqueness using shrinking length. Its proof is the standard endpoint-Cauchy/Cantor argument adapted to K-valued order distance.

This is a positive novelty determination, not an unsourced fallback: exact searches for the paired endpoints iota(n)t^{-1} and iota(1/(n+1)) found no established counterpart, and the asymmetric valuation-1/valuation-0 gap witness is a bespoke construction tailored to the preceding K page. Its truth-risk route was checked directly: the intervals are nonempty and nested; any common x would have v(x)>=1 from the upper endpoints and v(x)<1 from the lower endpoints; and every length retains a nonzero index-0 coefficient, so the shrinking theorem is not implicated. The proof is the local derivation of those facts.
